column5: almsgiving and cleansing
column6: Jesus answers concern with cleansing by telling his hearers to give alms and declaring all clean; this directly parallels the commentary's given share that purifies what remains.

column5: giving to poor; righteousness remains forever
column6: Paul joins scattering gifts to the poor with righteousness remaining forever; it combines the commentary's paid crop-share with its falāḥ and bāqī permanence.

column5: seed, bread, harvest of righteousness
column6: God supplies seed to the sower and bread for food, multiplies seed, and increases a harvest of righteousness; its gift context maps the commentary's blessed crop-growth to ethical fruit.

column5: firstfruits holy; whole batch holy
column6: Paul's firstfruits analogy makes the whole dough holy from its consecrated portion; it gives a precise cultic counterpart to the commentary's share whose giving cleanses the remainder.

column5: almsgiving atones for sin
column6: Sirach compares water quenching fire with almsgiving atoning for sin; it makes explicit the purificatory result assigned to tezekkā's charitable share.

column5: redeeming wrong by mercy to poor
column6: Daniel's Aramaic counsel tells the king to break off sins through righteousness and wrongs through mercy to the poor; it joins relief of need to moral rescue like the commentary's gift and purification.

column5: seventh-year field; needy eat its remnant
column6: The seventh-year field is left so needy people eat and animals take its remainder; it concretizes the commentary's harvested land as holding a claim beyond the owner's consumption.

column5: field corners and gleanings at harvest
column6: At reaping, field corners and gleanings must remain; this is a direct legal form of the commentary's crop-right owed at harvest.

column5: forgotten sheaf for vulnerable people; blessing
column6: A forgotten sheaf must remain for the alien, orphan, and widow so God blesses the work; it links surrendered harvest portion to blessing as the commentary links giving to purified productive remainder.

column5: annual tithe of field yield
column6: Israel must tithe all seed-yield of the field year by year; its stated annual crop measure closely meets the commentary's output-and-allotted-share facet.

column5: third-year tithe of produce distributed
column6: After completing the third-year tithe of produce, it is given to Levite, alien, orphan, and widow; its distribution specifies whom a crop due supports.

column5: firstfruits given; blessing on household
column6: Firstfruits and offerings given to priests make blessing rest on the household; it combines output-share and blessing in the commentary's z-k-w agricultural sequence.

column5: honor God with first produce
column6: Honoring the LORD from wealth and all first produce provides a concise biblical practice behind the commentary's payment from crop or wealth.

column5: barns filled and vats overflowing
column6: The verse pictures filled barns and overflowing vats after firstfruits; it supplies abundance as the outcome of offered produce, rather than generic prosperity.

column5: full tithe; heavens opened for blessing
column6: The full tithe is brought to the storehouse and God opens heaven to pour out blessing; it makes a fixed due share and divinely granted increase mutually explicit.

column5: firstfruits and tithes of produce
column6: Tobit carries firstfruits and tithes of produce to Jerusalem; the narrative embodies the commentary's zakāt-like harvest obligation in pious practice.

column5: third tenth for those in need
column6: Tobit's third tenth goes to people for whom he has a duty of care; it supplies the vulnerable-recipient side of the commentary's harvest share.

column5: firstfruits of winepress and threshing floor
column6: The Didache directs firstfruits from winepress, threshing floor, cattle, and sheep to prophets; it carries the commentary's harvest-due motif into early Christian community order.

column5: firstfruits given to poor
column6: If no prophet is present, the Didache directs firstfruits to the poor; it makes the crop share a relief obligation, not private purification alone.

column4: Basil of Caesarea, Homily 6 on Luke 12:18
column5: hoarded grain and the poor
column6: Basil reads the rich man's larger barns as hoarding surplus that belongs with the needy; this Christian interpretation makes explicit the commentary's alternative between a harvest shared and one retained for self.

column5: larger barns for all grain and goods
column6: The rich man demolishes barns to store all his grain and goods; against the commentary's harvest-day due, it stages productive output withheld for self.

column5: alms; unfailing heavenly treasure
column6: Jesus commands almsgiving and calls the resulting heavenly treasury unfailing; it directly associates relinquished share with the commentary's better and more-lasting outcome.

column5: rain-soaked land; useful crop; blessing
column6: Land that has drunk repeated rain produces a crop useful to its cultivators and receives God's blessing; it closely matches the commentary's worked, growing field rather than mere pasture.

column5: thorns and thistles; curse and burning
column6: The contrasting land bears thorns and thistles and approaches curse and burning; it gives an ethical version of the commentary's same-ground contrast between productive cultivation and vegetation headed for ruin.

column5: digging, clearing, planting; expected fruit
column6: The vineyard-owner digs, clears stones, plants, and expects good grapes; divine care of a cultivated plot renders concrete the commentary's agricultural sense assigned to Rabb.

column5: no pruning or hoeing; briers; no rain
column6: The ruined vineyard will neither be pruned nor hoed, so briers arise and rain is withheld; it is the inverse of the commentary's ploughed, watered, yielding field.

column5: vineyard expected justice and righteousness
column6: Isaiah identifies the LORD's vineyard with Israel and its expected fruit with justice and righteousness; it makes the commentary's agricultural success an explicitly moral outcome.

column5: LORD as vineyard keeper watering and guarding
column6: The LORD calls himself the vineyard's keeper, watering it continually and guarding it night and day; this closely clarifies the commentary's farm-steward sense of Rabb.

column5: sow righteousness; reap loyal love; break fallow ground
column6: Hosea commands sowing righteousness, reaping loyal love, and breaking fallow ground while seeking the LORD; agricultural labor becomes the ethical transformation that the commentary casts as purification and lasting success.

column5: rain waters earth; sprouting; seed and bread
column6: Rain and snow water the earth, make it sprout, and provide seed and bread; this gives a precise biblical water-to-growth-to-food field scene beside the commentary's expanded field imagery.

column5: rain in season; land produce and tree fruit
column6: God's timely rain makes land yield produce and trees fruit; it places the commentary's crop growth under divine blessing.

column5: blade, head, full grain
column6: Jesus's seed parable narrates the ordered growth of blade, head, and full grain; it gives a kingdom reading of the commentary's field-process.

column5: ripe grain; sickle; harvest
column6: When the grain permits, the sickle is sent because harvest has arrived; it supplies the harvest-stage after the commentary's growth and cultivation.

column5: good soil bears fruit with endurance
column6: Good soil is an honest, good heart that holds the word and bears fruit with endurance; it joins the commentary's cultivated crop to falāḥ as lasting in good.

column5: worldly care and wealth choke fruit
column6: Worldly care and wealth are thorns that choke the word and make it unfruitful; this concretely meets the commentary's contrast between a worldly field and a fruitful, enduring one.

column5: Father as vinedresser
column6: Jesus calls the Father the vinedresser; this is a direct Christian agricultural analogue for the commentary's Rabb who maintains and restores a farm.

column5: pruning cleans fruitful branches for more fruit
column6: The vinedresser removes barren branches and prunes fruit-bearing ones so they bear more; it puts cleansing and maintenance directly inside a growth-to-fruit process.

column5: unabiding branch withers and is burned
column6: A branch that does not remain withers and is gathered for fire; it supplies a pointed vegetal reverse to the commentary's crop that remains in good rather than becoming ruined growth.

column5: sowing to flesh or Spirit; corruption or eternal life
column6: The two sowings culminate in corruption or eternal life; it gives direct field language to the commentary's contrast between a worldly crop and an afterlife-directed one.

column5: do good; reap in due season; do not give up
column6: Doing good is to continue because one will reap in due season without giving up; it closely supplies the commentary's success as remaining in good.

column5: harvested fruit for eternal life
column6: The reaper gathers fruit for eternal life, so sower and reaper rejoice together; it makes harvest an image of the enduring good emphasized at 87:17.

column5: farmer waits for precious fruit and rains
column6: The farmer waits patiently for the earth's precious fruit and its rains while believers await the Lord; this connects crop maturation to the commentary's enduring, eschatological good.

column5: fruitful tree; leaf does not wither; prospers
column6: The righteous person is a watered tree yielding fruit whose leaf does not wither and whose work prospers; it is a close vegetal counterpart to cultivated success and permanence.

column5: watered tree does not cease bearing fruit
column6: The tree by water stays green through heat and drought and does not cease producing fruit; it directly contrasts durable blessed growth with the commentary's perishing pasture.

column5: break fallow ground; do not sow among thorns
column6: Jeremiah's call to break fallow ground and avoid sowing among thorns applies ploughing to repentance; it strengthens the commentary's ethical reading of broken soil and fruitful cultivation.

column5: God teaches the farmer right practice
column6: In Isaiah's farming instruction, the farmer's God teaches him the right practice; it offers an indirect biblical counterpart to the commentary's Lord who tends and orders a farm.

column5: seed dies in order to live
column6: The commentary uses a seed smothered under soil as purification's opposite, whereas Paul makes a sown seed's death the necessary image of resurrection; the opposed agricultural valuation is the link.

column5: earth's ripe harvest and final reaping
column6: The angel announces that the earth's harvest is ripe and must be reaped; it supplies an explicitly final-harvest horizon for the commentary's crop and afterlife contrast.

column5: Arabic ف ل ح; Hebrew פלח; cleaving ground
column6: The commentary's Arabic ف ل ح is developed as splitting and ploughing soil; Hebrew פֹּלֵחַ depicts cleaving the ground in the psalm's simile, retaining the same concrete root-scene in a different setting.

column5: pe'ah as an unfixed harvest obligation
column6: The Mishnah lists pe'ah, the field-edge left from harvest, among obligations with no fixed measure; this legal reception sharpens the commentary's claim that produce bears a due share.

column5: charity saving from Gehenna
column6: Rabbi Akiva's defense of supporting the poor makes charity a means by which the giver is saved from Gehenna; it develops the commentary's charitable purification into a salvation claim.

column5: deeds as roots that withstand the wind
column6: Avot compares deeds exceeding wisdom to a deeply rooted tree that wind cannot uproot; its moral agriculture gives a Jewish image for the commentary's remaining in good.

column5: vine and elm; rich support poor
column6: Hermas makes the fruitful vine depend on the otherwise fruitless elm, then reads their mutual support as rich and poor aiding one another; it turns agricultural fruit into a specific charity relation.

column5: hardworking farmer's first share of crops
column6: The hard-working farmer ought first to receive a share of the crops; this provides a distinct New Testament use of cultivation, labor, and a rightful portion beside the commentary's farmer and yield.

column5: Arabic ز ك و and Hebrew זכה; cleansing hands
column6: If Hebrew זכה is accepted as cognate with the commentary's Arabic ز ك و label, Job's cleansing of the hands supplies a physical-purity use; the cognacy and semantic scope need verification.
